entities.name: The Divine Comedy
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Divine Comedy is an Italian narrative poem by Dante Alighieri, begun c. 1308 and completed c. 1321, shortly before his death. Widely considered the pre-eminent work in Italian literature and one of the greatest poems in world literature, it describes Dante's imaginary journey through Hell (Inferno), Purgatory (Purgatorio), and Paradise (Paradiso), guided first by the Roman poet Virgil and then by his beloved Beatrice.

The poem synthesizes the entirety of medieval Christian learning into a narrative of the soul's journey toward God. Dante drew on Aristotle, Aquinas, Ptolemaic astronomy, biblical prophecy, and the politics of 14th-century Italy, populating Hell with his political enemies and Paradise with the saints and philosophers he most admired. The Inferno's 34 cantos include the most famous passages — the Gates of Hell ('Abandon all hope, ye who enter here'), the story of Paolo and Francesca, and the frozen lake of Satan — that have become part of Western cultural consciousness.

The Divine Comedy's cultural significance is almost immeasurable. It established Italian (Tuscan) as a literary language capable of matching Latin, effectively creating modern Italian. Its theology shaped popular Christian eschatology for centuries. It inspired Botticelli's illustrations, Michelangelo's Last Judgment, T.S. Eliot's The Waste Land, and James Joyce's Ulysses. More than 700 years after its composition, it remains among the most widely read, studied, and translated medieval texts, with over 80 complete translations into English alone.
